text: Across 715 overlapping 20-year stretches of US consumer prices starting each month from 1947 to 2006, an annuity check that rises 2% a year kept its starting buying power in only 2.4% of them (17 windows, all starting 1947-1949).
Over 25-year stretches it kept up in 0.0%.
Median inflation over 20 years was 3.1% a year, so after 20 raises the 2% check typically bought 80.7% of what its first check bought (level check: 54.3%).
In the worst stretch (starting 1966) it bought 43.1%.
In the latest full stretch, Aug 2006 to Aug 2026, the 2% check ended at 90.4% of its starting buying power and a level check at 60.9%.
A 2% raise slows the loss of buying power; historically it almost never stopped it.

The data show the 2% raise was partial protection in essentially every period since the late 1940s, including the low-inflation 2000s and 2010s: it narrows the gap with a level check but does not keep purchasing power steady.
It kept up in 17 of 715 windows; say 'almost never since the late 1940s' and give the count.
'Inflation averages 3.1%.' It is the median 20-year rate of 1947-2026 windows, not an expectation.
